title: Everything else
intro:
# Everything else

The odds and ends: everything Black can play on move one that the earlier chapters do not cover. One safe recipe each, and none of them needs much memorising.

## The Dutch, 1...f5

The one that changes something. Look at the b1 to h7 diagonal: the pawn on f5 sits right across it, so the bishop on d3 would be staring at its own dead end. The bishop goes to e2 instead.

After that it is the King's Indian recipe. Black has no pawn on d5, so take the space with c4, castle early because Black's whole plan is a kingside attack, and meet ...Ne4 by challenging it with Nc3.

## 1...c5, and the one exception to bishop first

This is the only line in the repertoire where e3 comes before Bf4, and it is worth knowing why rather than remembering it. Black has played ...c5 without ...d5, so the c7 square is already empty. That makes ...Qb6 stronger than usual, and it also means ...cxd4 comes without the loss of time that normally makes it harmless.

So play 2.e3, take back on d4 with the e-pawn, and bring the bishop out next move with a solid centre already behind it. One move later, and nothing lost.

## 1...b6, 1...e6, 1...g6

Nothing changes. Bishop out, triangle, knight, castle. With ...b6 or ...e6 the bishop goes to d3 as usual, because the h7 diagonal is clear. With ...g6, wait one move: if Black follows with ...d6 you are in chapter 3, and if ...d5, chapter 4.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Putting the bishop on d3 against the Dutch, where a pawn on f5 blocks it. Playing 2.Bf4 against 1...c5 out of habit and having to solve problems that e3 would have prevented. Reaching for a different opening, an early e4 or c4, because the position looks unfamiliar. Starting a kingside attack before castling, which the Dutch punishes harder than anything else.

tree.note: The Dutch. Black grabs e4 and plans a kingside attack, at the cost of loosening the king.

children.note: The same first move as ever. The bishop is outside the pawn chain before anything else happens.

mistakes.note: A real anti-Dutch try, hitting the squares Black has weakened. It is a different opening to learn, and this repertoire does not need one.
The gambit is playable but sharp, and it throws away the setup you actually know.
Attacking with the pawn in front of your own king before a single piece is out.

children.note: Build the triangle. Nothing about the Dutch changes the first three moves.
Develop and cover e5 and g5, the squares Black would like for a knight.

mistakes.note: Look at the diagonal: the pawn on f5 sits right across it. The bishop would be aiming at its own dead end.
It blocks the c-pawn, and against the Dutch the pawn wants c4.

children.note: Here the bishop goes to e2 for a different reason than usual: the pawn on f5 blocks the d3 diagonal completely, so d3 would be a wasted square.

mistakes.note: The habit from the ...d5 chapters. The pawn on f5 makes that diagonal useless while it stands there.
Also good and the pawn is going there. Getting the pieces out first keeps things simple.

children.note: Castle before doing anything else. Black's whole plan is a kingside attack, so the king wants to be tucked away and the rook on f1 wants to be behind the f-pawn.

mistakes.note: Too early, and with the king in the centre Black gets ...Nc6 and ...d6 with tempo.
Useful, but the Dutch does not usually come with ...Nh5, so castling matters more here.

children.note: Black prepares ...e5, the break that gives the Dutch its play.
Black has no pawn on d5, so take the space, exactly as against the King's Indian setups.

mistakes.note: Too modest. Nothing is contesting the centre, so c4 is free space.
The square is not covered yet: ...dxe5 wins a knight for a pawn whichever way White recaptures.

children.note: The standard Dutch square, and here the pawn on f5 is holding it. That changes what White should do about it.
Do not chase it. The knight on e4 is defended by the f5 pawn, so Nc3 only invites ...Nxc3 and a wrecked queenside. Play a move you want anyway and let Black show what the knight is worth.

mistakes.note: The natural challenge, and it is the one move that helps Black: ...Nxc3 leaves White with doubled c-pawns and nothing to show for them.
The right way to challenge the knight, just a move early. Slipping h3 in first costs nothing and Black cannot improve much in the meantime.
Same answer as a move ago: ...dxe5 and White has given a knight for a pawn. The outpost needs a defender first.

children.note: Black develops the bishop, which is the piece the Dutch usually struggles with.
Now challenge it, and with this knight. Trading on d2 lets White take back with a piece rather than a pawn, so the queenside stays whole.

mistakes.note: Still the wrong knight. Taking back on c3 with a pawn is exactly what Black wants.

children.note: Take with the queen. The knight on b1 stays where it is, the pawns are untouched, and the queen is well placed behind the centre.

mistakes.note: Also fine. The queen recapture keeps the b1 knight free to choose its square later.

children.plan: Play Nc3 or Nd2 with the other knight, then Rad1 and look for the e4 or d5 break. Black attack needs ...g5, which loosens a king you can already reach down the d-file.
children.name: The Dutch, 1...f5

children.note: Black trades before the knight is pushed back: on e4 it was the best piece, and there was no good way to keep it there.
Black castles, completing the setup. The plan is ...d6, ...Qe8 and a slow kingside build.
The modest square, as usual in the classical Dutch: castle first, expand later.
Black opens the bishop's diagonal and gets ready to castle: the classical Dutch shape.
The knight develops and holds the e4 square, which the whole Dutch setup is built around.

tree.note: Straight at d4 before White has built anything. This is the one place the bishop does not come out first.

children.note: The exception to the rule, and worth knowing why. After 2.Bf4 Black has ...Qb6 hitting b2 and d4 at once, and also ...cxd4 winning the pawn back on good terms, because the c7 square is already empty. Hold the centre first and the bishop comes out next move.

mistakes.note: The usual move, but here ...cxd4 is awkward: taking back with the queen invites ...Nc6 with tempo, and ...Qb6 comes with an extra threat because c7 is free.
It hands Black the centre and a free developing move with ...e6 and ...Bxc5.
A real alternative that turns the game into a Benoni. It is sound and it is a different opening.

children.note: Take towards the centre. Now the bishop can come to f4 with the pawn on d4 already solid.

mistakes.note: The queen comes out early and ...Nc6 chases it straight away.

children.note: Now the bishop comes out, one move later than usual and none the worse for it.

mistakes.note: It hits d5 and is perfectly sound, but it leaves this repertoire behind.

children.note: Back to the normal plan: knight, bishop, castle.
children.plan: Play Bd3 or Be2, castle, and hold d4 with c3. The pawn on d4 is isolated in some lines, so keep pieces on it and remember the e5 square is yours.
children.name: The ...c5 first move

children.note: Normal development in a normal position: the sting of 1...c5 has gone.
Black stakes the centre in return, and the position becomes a quiet, symmetrical one.
Black takes at once: the point of 1...c5 is to trade off White's centre pawn early.

tree.note: Black fianchettos on the queenside and leaves the centre alone for now.

children.note: Nothing here needs a new idea. The bishop comes out and the setup follows.

mistakes.note: Taking the whole centre is good chess and a well known answer to ...b6. It is also not the London.
The c-pawn wants its square, and Black has done nothing to make you hurry.

children.note: Build the triangle. The bishop on b7 is aiming at g2 and a pawn on e3 does not care.
Develop, and look at what it stops: the knight on f3 blocks the b7 bishop road to g2. Until it is there, the g2 pawn is only defended by the bishop on f1.

mistakes.note: It hangs g2. The bishop on f1 was the only thing defending it, and the bishop on b7 is looking straight down that diagonal: ...Bxg2 wins a pawn and the rook is next. Play Nf3 first and the diagonal is shut.

children.note: Here d3 is right: the diagonal to h7 is clear and Black will castle into it.

mistakes.note: Passive. There is no pawn on g6 or f5, so the bishop should take the diagonal that matters.

children.note: The last minor piece, keeping c3 free for the pawn.
children.plan: Castle, play c3, then Ne5 and f4 as usual. Black's bishop on b7 is looking at a pawn on d5 that is not there yet, so it is the quieter piece.
children.name: The ...b6 fianchetto

children.note: The quiet square again: Black finishes developing and will castle next.
Development continues. Black delays the d-pawn, keeping both ...d5 and ...d6 in reserve.
Black opens the other bishop's diagonal and keeps the centre flexible.
The bishop goes straight to the long diagonal, the whole idea of 1...b6: pressure on e4 and the centre from the side.

tree.note: A fianchetto is coming, so the answer depends on the d-pawn.

children.note: Bishop out, and the d-pawn tells you the rest.

mistakes.note: Taking the centre is good and it is not this repertoire.
The pawn lunge against a fianchetto, before any development. Black castles and opens the centre.

children.note: Build the triangle and wait one more move.
children.plan: If Black plays ...d6, you are in chapter 3: bishop to e2 and take the centre with c4. If ...d5, you are in chapter 4: bishop to e2 and hold with c3.
children.name: The ...g6 fianchetto

children.note: The fianchetto completes. Which chapter this becomes still depends on the d-pawn.

tree.note: A waiting move. It usually becomes a position from chapter 1, or a Dutch if ...f5 follows.

children.note: Bishop out first, then see what Black has in mind.

mistakes.note: This is a French Defence, which is fine chess and a whole other opening.

children.note: The triangle again. Black is yet to say anything about the centre.
children.plan: If Black plays ...d5 you are in chapter 1. If ...f5, you are in the Dutch above and the bishop goes to e2. If ...b6, play Bd3 and carry on.
children.name: The ...e6 move order

children.note: Black develops flexibly. This can still become a classical ...d5 game, a Dutch with ...f5, or a queenside fianchetto.
